speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) whether the Ministry can clarify how the additional certificates of entitlement (COEs) over the next few years will not exacerbate traffic congestion; (b) what alternative measures are being considered to prevent any unintended increases in road density; and (c) whether the "cut and fill" approach will continue or whether a more sustainable system can be developed to maintain a balanced COE quota.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) whether the Ministry will review the current zero percent allowable vehicle growth rate, given that ERP 2.0's system is expected to allow the authorities to better manage traffic congestion; (b) whether the Ministry assesses that the planned injection of 20,000 COEs will help to stabilise COE prices during the years where COE quota is in short supply; and (c) if so, whether more details can be shared.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) in light of the imminent implementation of Electronic Road Pricing 2.0, whether there are any plans to revise the Vehicle Quota System for the total number of automobile COEs issued over the full 10 years; (b) whether the Ministry has conducted any study on what the anticipated impact on COE prices will be; (c) if so, whether the details of such study can be shared; and (d) if not, whether there are plans to conduct such a study.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) whether the Ministry will review the current level of electric vehicle (EV) subsidies particularly as cheaper models enter the market given that EVs still contribute to carbon emissions through power generation; (b) whether LTA's goal remains for Singapore to go car-lite or has the primary focus shifted to be on transitioning from petrol cars to EVs; and (c) what active steps, beyond expanding the public transport network, are being taken to discourage overall car usage.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Members have raised two broad categories of questions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The second is about the impact of electric vehicle (EV) subsidies on COE prices.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On the injection of additional COEs, Ms He Ting Ru asked if this aligns with Singapore’s car-lite vision, while Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the impact on traffic congestion.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Melvin Yong and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked if we could review the total size of our vehicle population, given the capabilities of Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) 2.0 to better manage congestion.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government remains committed to Singapore’s car-lite vision, where walk, cycle, ride, particularly the use of public transport, are the predominant travel modes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is necessary given our land and carbon constraints.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we rely mainly on private vehicles to meet our mobility needs, we will face severe traffic congestion and gridlock, like what some overseas cities are experiencing.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As roads already take up about 12% of our total land area, we cannot keep on building more and more roads, because that will take away land from other important needs such as housing, hospitals and schools.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Next, an accessible and affordable mass public transport network is the central pillar of our car-lite vision.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Compared to other transport options, mass public transport enables the greatest number of people to get to their destinations with the least land take and carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is why we have and will continue to make significant investments in our public transport infrastructure through upgrading and expanding our rail and bus networks, and subsidising public transport journeys for commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Roads and vehicles will complement our public transport infrastructure and offer additional transport options for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Having a car-lite vision does not mean that our total car population cannot increase.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The key is to avoid road congestion through the use of both ownership controls and usage-based pricing, which is what we have been doing over the last few decades.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The ERP gantries at arterial roads, including the one in my constituency at Toa Payoh Lorong 5, have also been switched off since the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: An increase in the vehicle population does not automatically lead to an increase in the total vehicular usage, as there are car owners who may choose to take public transport to work, as well as those who use their cars mostly on weekends or during off-peak hours.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is why it is useful to have both ownership controls and usage-based pricing, so that we can enable some families to own cars while keeping congestion in check, especially during peak periods.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This allows for more flexible and responsive congestion management.
The additional COEs will give us more flexibility to meet this commitment and further increase the COE supply in the next few quarters before we reach the peak supply from 2026.
LTA will continue to closely monitor traffic conditions and, where necessary, adjust ERP charges to keep traffic congestion in check.
We have not made a decision on whether to implement distance-based charging, though ERP 2.0 gives us the option to do so.
We will need to study this further, including with the data from ERP 2.0, as there are trade-offs we need to think through carefully.
Mr Melvin Yong asked if the planned injection would help to stabilise COE prices.
COE prices are a function of supply and demand.
We have introduced measures to increase supply since last year, including "cut and fill" and now the additional injection.
However, we are not able to predict how prices will move as that would also depend on the demand from motorists.
If we look back at how prices and demand factors have changed since we increased COE supply from late last year, there are some observations which I would like to share with the House.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The proportion of bids won by foreigners remains low and has decreased to about 2% this year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The proportion won by car leasing companies, which bid for vehicles that are then leased out as Private Hire Cars, or PHCs, has also decreased from 26% in 2022 when COE prices were relatively lower, to about 10% this year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The decrease in the proportion of bids won by car leasing companies also illustrates why the suggestion of having a separate COE category for PHCs and moving existing quota from Cat A and B into this separate category, is not a straightforward exercise.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Demand for COE from car leasing companies can vary quite a bit from quarter to quarter and from year to year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is difficult to ascertain upfront the quota required to meet the needs of point-to-point drivers and commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I explained in this House previously, if we move too much of the existing quota from Cat A and B to this new category for PHCs, it would reduce the supply in Cat A and B vis-a-vis the demand from non-PHC buyers and could lead to an increase in COE prices in these categories.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On the other hand, if we underestimated the quota to be moved to the separate category for PHCs, it would lead to insufficient PHC supply which would in turn cause an increase in PHC prices and reduce accessibility for point-to-point commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are the difficult trade-offs and it is not a straightforward exercise.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This amount is deducted off the Additional Registration Fee when registering a new electric car.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The subsidies are intended to reduce the difference in the total cost of ownership between a mass market electric car and its internal combustion engine (ICE) and hybrid equivalents.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In many instances, the upfront cost of an electric car remains slightly above an ICE or hybrid equivalent even after the EV subsidies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: With this context, please allow me to clarify a few points.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, the demand of COE is driven by how many people want to buy cars.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It does not matter whether the buyer is buying an electric, ICE or hybrid car.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But when someone decides to buy a car, the EV subsidies serve to nudge him or her towards considering an electric car, instead of an ICE car.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is because without such subsidies, the electric car will be more expensive than its ICE equivalent at this time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The price difference may narrow and even disappear in future, when technology evolves and EV prices decrease further.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: EV subsidies on their own do not induce new demand for cars.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They are intended to encourage a car buyer to consider buying an electric car instead of an ICE or hybrid car, by reducing the upfront costs of an electric car.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, it is a business decision for motor dealers when they decide how to price their vehicles, electric or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The COE is an input cost to the dealers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If they submit higher COE bids than what they had included in their pricing, it will eat into their profit margins.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Hence, there is no commercial incentive for electric car dealers to excessively mark up their prices or bid for higher COE just because of the EV subsidies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Marking up their prices by too much will affect their competitiveness versus other car brands, while bidding for higher COE will erode their profit margins.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We acknowledge the concerns about how some higher-end cars have lowered their engine capacity and power ratings to come under Cat A instead of Cat B.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Members including Mr Ang Wei Neng, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Leong Mun Wai had previously asked if we could determine the COE category using the vehicle's Open Market Value.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We understand the rationale of this suggestion and will continue to review our criteria as technology and market trends evolve.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have some supplementary questions for Question Nos 3 and 6.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For Question No 3, if traffic congestion exceeds anticipated levels after issuing additional COEs, will the Ministry consider a mid-term review to potentially adjust the COE supply?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Ministry plan to stay agile and responsive to unexpected congestion increases in real time?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For Question No 6, the EV transition is progressing but there are concerns that a shift from petrol or ICE to electric cars might reduce the urgency to go car-lite.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry elaborate on how it ensures that the EV transition does not detract from its car-lite goal?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What specific targets or metrics are in place to measure success towards the car-lite vision versus just transiting between different vehicle types?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If there are certain stretches of roads that require intervention, we can do so through the use of usage-based pricing.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: With ERP 2.0, we no longer need to set up a physical gantry.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We can more quickly and in a more responsive manner introduce virtual gantries, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On the second question, I wanted to clarify, Sir, that a car-lite vision does not mean no cars.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It also does not mean that we want to reduce the total car population.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What we want to manage is the congestion.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Importantly, we want to also continue to invest in our public transport network, both MRT and bus, building more MRT lines.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Bus Connectivity Enhancement Programme will allow us to introduce more bus services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Even for car owners, they may decide not to drive their car during peak hours or during weekdays.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They may park their car at home and then use public transport.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, car-lite, we should look at it in that perspective.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is about increasing the walk-cycle-ride and the public transport mode share.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The LTA had cited reduced car usage patterns, in part, driven by flexible work arrangements as one of the reasons that we are now able to inject an additional 20,000 COEs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With companies making moves to mandate a return-to-office policy, how would this affect LTA's planning assumption?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I understand the Minister has already said that it is still being studied.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But what are the key considerations in deciding to implement or not implement distance-based charging, given that ERP 2.0 already has the capacity to do so?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are trends which can change over time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Certainly, we have to carefully monitor the road usage and the traffic patterns, with or without the injection of these additional COEs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because, as we know, even at this moment, we still do not see a need to turn on the ERP gantries entering into the CBD or in the arterial roads.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This assessment is arrived at, based on that careful monitoring of road conditions and travel speeds.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If, indeed, there is a change, whether it is due to removal of flexible work arrangements or other reasons, then we will have to respond accordingly using this tool that we have, which is usage-based pricing.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: ERP 2.0 gives us additional capabilities to do so in a more responsive and quicker manner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I certainly hope that the companies that are asking their employees to come back to work in the office would also remember that while there may be some benefits of coming back to work, I think a lot of employees do appreciate flexi-work arrangements to have a better work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In some instances, it can also be more productive.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, in the public sector, for example, we have implemented flexi-work and it is something which we hope can continue, because it is appreciated and welcomed by our public officers.
The second question on distance-based charging and what are some of the considerations, I mentioned in my main reply that it is a difficult set of trade-offs.
There are different stakeholder groups that will be affected differently when we implement distance-based charging – of course, depending on how we design the charges.
It is still too early for me to go into the details, but we do recognise that there could be certain groups of drivers who need to drive for work purposes and they travel longer distances.
So, what is the impact on this group?
That is one of the key considerations that we are looking at in designing the distance-based charging policies.
We want to look at it because it is one of the tools that will allow us to calibrate between ownership control and usage-based pricing.
So, we can relax on the ownership controls, but then you have to tighten up on the usage-based pricing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second supplementary question requires just a little bit of context, so, if you provide me a little indulgence on preamble.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The introduction of ERP 2.0 will presumably reduce the intensity of car usage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The estimates published by MOT suggest something in the order of 6%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, this will certainly open the scope for increasing the total vehicle quotas without necessarily increasing congestion, as Minister Chee has mentioned, which in turn would potentially allow for a greater number of COEs with less impact on prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, this could mean lower COE prices if we choose not to increase the quota.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, I think it is very valuable for this House to know what MOT's position is on the total number, or at least if the direction, an increase or decrease in the carrying capacity of cars, if a specific number is not forthcoming.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Maybe I could just hear from Assoc Prof Lim what he meant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, very quickly, my understanding is that the total number of vehicles currently in the vehicle quota system is something in the order of one million in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, the question, in a sense, is that with ERP 2.0, if the intensity of usage falls, whether we could allow for the possibility of an increase in that total number, or if we do not, then naturally that reduced usage would also imply a reduction in COE prices.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The intent that we explained when we did the "cut and fill" last year, was indeed to try and reduce the peak-to-trough ratio.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are not doing this injection only because of the 6%.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think the 6% reduction in the vehicular usage is one factor.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For that, I would not link it to ERP 2.0 per se.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think it is more driven by the changes in the travel patterns after COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we look at distance-based charging as an additional usage-based pricing tool, that will give us further leeway to do that.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are looking at different usage-based pricing tools to avoid congestion.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we are confident in achieving that outcome, then increasing the car population by relaxing ownership controls would not be a worry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I was just looking at Table 1 where the quota premium has come down by 4% to 21% compared to a year ago.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, if you look at Table 2, the Cat A and Cat B COE bids won by car leasing companies have also come down from about 24% to 26% in 2022 and 2023, to about 10% in 2024 as of October.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would this not then suggest that the car leasing companies do actually have an influence on the quota premiums?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If I were to look back at 2012 when LTA made the decision to remove taxi companies from the COE bidding process, they have also stated that the taxi operators' influence on COE prices is actually observed from them taking up a larger proportion, up to 25%, of Cat A COEs back then.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, this is one indication that the main driver for the increase in the COE price is unlikely to be due to the PHC car leasing companies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Having said that, I am certainly not saying that they do not contribute to the overall demand.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the point I am making is, what are the key drivers that are contributing to the increase in demand?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What I have also explained in my main reply is that if we look at having a separate category – we are not ruling out that possibility, we are studying it.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, I hope Mr Chua agrees with me on this, that by having a separate category, it does not mean that you have suddenly got a windfall of COE supply dropping from the sky.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It means you have to transfer existing quotas from Cat A and Cat B to this new category.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that process of deciding how much to transfer is not so straightforward.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We did it for taxis, but there is a difference between taxis and PHCs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: PHCs, some of them, or in fact, quite a number of them, are used also as private vehicles by the owners.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They come in part-time during peak hours, for example, but during other parts of the day, they may use it as a private vehicle.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it is not so clear-cut that these are just point-to-point vehicles or private vehicles – it is a bit of a hybrid, they use it for dual purposes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because of that, it is not so easy to ascertain what is this total number that would then fit into this separate category, if we decide to have a separate category.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that is one of the challenges that we face.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is in deciding what would be the amount that you need to transfer in terms of the supply to this new separate category.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And so, it is something that I think we need to take a look at carefully.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If there are other ways to address the concerns with COE supply, we should also be open to looking at those other options too.
